summary: AE + SE walkthrough of Redwood edge-case capabilities focused on long-context workloads (~100k-200k tokens), high TPS scenarios, streaming behavior under backpressure, and timeout mitigation. Customer concerned about latency vs cost, retries and graceful degradation, VPC/KMS requirements, and benchmark methodology. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send pricing and SOC2/VPC docs, SE to provide benchmark scripts and proposed test plan, customer to share traffic profile and sample payloads.

transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE; with me is Jonah our SE. Quick intros?
[00:10] Sarah: Sarah Lopez, CTO at Aperture Analytics. We're mainly interested in inference throughput and handling very long customer contexts, plus security.
[00:18] Maya: Awesome. Jonah, want to set expectations?
[00:22] Jonah: Yeah, we'll run through the Console and API, then deep dive on 3 edgecases: long context, high TPS, streaming backpressure and timeouts. We'll surface config levers and benchmarking suggestions.
[00:35] Mark: Quick note, our traffic is bursty - short spikes up to 1k rps, sustained 200-400 rps for minutes. Contexts can reach 100k tokens for legal docs.
[00:44] Jonah: Great, that's the kind of profile we built the demo around.
[00:48] [01:05] Jonah: (screen share) Here's the Redwood Console, route configs, model catalog - note we've got quantized variants and long-context variants. For 100k tokens we recommend long-context model family with offloading and kv cache tuning.
[01:20] Priya: When you say offloading, is that disk swap or CPU? Last time we saw huge latency with swap.
[01:26] Jonah: Good question — in Redwood Dedicated we prefer KV offload to high-bandwidth NVMe managed by the runtime, not general-purpose swap. It avoids OS-level thrashing. That said, performance depends on sequence distribution and you still pay a latency tax for misses.
[01:40] Sarah: How do you estimate cost for those huge contexts? Tokens blow up.
[01:45] Maya: We'll include tokenized cost estimates in the follow-up but high-context workloads favor batching and prefix-KV caching to avoid recomputing the whole context. Also, model selection (quantization) affects unit cost.
[01:57] [02:20] Jonah: Now TPS: here's a simulated client sending 800 rps burst to a dedicated pool. Redwood's autoscaler supports buffer-based scaling and can route to warm spare capacity to absorb spikes. The runtime has hedging and backpressure hooks so clients can be signaled.
[02:36] Mark: What's the default timeout behavior on streaming responses? We saw random timeouts during spikes.
[02:42] Jonah: Streaming timeouts usually result from backpressure if the runtime's internal queues are full or network congested. We surface retryable vs non-retryable errors; for streaming we recommend client-side windowed reads and an exponential backoff for reconnect with resume tokens so you don't restart the entire generation.
[02:58] Priya: Resume tokens, can we get that with the host API?
[03:02] Jonah: Yes, we support chunked KV and resumable streaming in the API; the client SDK exposes a resume token so you can continue from the last acknowledged token. There's some complexity for deterministic outputs but for most applications it's fine.
[03:20] [03:40] Sarah: Any limits on resume windows or how far back you can resume?
[03:44] Jonah: We keep a sliding window based on cache TTLs and memory constraints; typical window is a few minutes or N tokens depending on config. For Dedicated you can extend those TTLs if you're willing to pay for larger KV caches.
[03:58] Maya: On the security side - Aperture asked about SOC2, KMS, and VPC connectivity.
[04:05] Sarah: Yes, and audit logs retention.
[04:08] Maya: We'll send SOC2 docs; for Private/Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS and VPC peering with optional on-prem connectors. Audit logs are available via the Console and can be exported to S3 or your SIEM.
[04:20] Mark: Do you anonymize logs by default? We need PII redaction before logs land in external storage.
[04:26] Jonah: We provide token-level masking rules and can integrate pre-ingestion redaction. That typically sits in your edge proxy or in the RW pipeline. We'll document the options.
[04:40] [05:00] Jonah: Back to performance: here's a flamegraph of token latency at 200k context under various kernels. Notice the KV fetch spikes at the start of generation. We mitigate by prefix caching and warm-starting sequences.
[05:18] Priya: How deterministic is warm-start? We worry about cache consistency across nodes.
[05:22] Jonah: Runtime manages KV sharding with consistent hashing and versions; we provide cache invalidation APIs and can do sticky routing for sessions that require strong locality. There's an availability vs cost tradeoff.
[05:38] Sarah: On dedicated vs hosted — what's the SLA bump?
[05:42] Maya: Dedicated comes with an SLA on throughput and latency tiers and reserved capacity; hosted is best-effort with usage limits. Dedicated also allows higher KV cache quotas and longer TTLs, which helps long-context workloads.
[05:56] [06:10] Mark: During spikes we saw 5-10% of streams drop with the competitor. How does Redwood avoid that?
[06:16] Jonah: Two parts: 1) Smart routing — requests hit warm nodes first and fallback policies route to compatible model variants rather than failing; 2) Streaming backpressure — we provide an explicit ACK-based flow control so slow clients don't pile up. If queue depth grows we can shed low-priority requests gracefully.
[06:34] Priya: Is that shedding configurable per tenant? We need to ensure premium routes never get shed.
[06:39] Jonah: Yes, per-route QoS and priority gating. We'll include sample policies in the docs.
[06:50] [07:10] Sarah: Can we run the benchmark here? I know we planned a separate POC but curious to see a micro-run.
[07:15] Maya: We can run a short synthetic now. Jonah, can you kick off the harness?
[07:20] Jonah: Starting a 5-minute pulse: 1k rps burst, 300 rps sustain, payloads with 80k token prefixes.
[07:30] [07:58] (noise, short pause while harness runs)
[08:02] Jonah: Early result — 95thpct token latency rose to ~1.6s during spike, end-to-end generation times varied; tail correlates with KV misses. Throughput recovered via warm spare routing.
[08:18] Mark: That's not bad — can you break down cost implications of warm spare capacity? We don't want to pay full time for idle capacity.
[08:26] Maya: Reserved burst pools are charged at a smaller premium; you can configure burst windows and pre-empt low-priority workloads during spikes. We'll model cost in the follow up.
[08:36] [09:00] Priya: About timeouts — how often should clients expect to hit them? We've seen timeouts when upstream proxies close idle streams.
[09:08] Jonah: Timeout rate depends on network path and client-side settings. Best practice: keep-alive windows, client windowed reads, resume tokens, and increase server-side send-timeout thresholds for long streams. For proxy issues we recommend tuning idle timeouts and use chunked transfer encoding.
[09:24] Sarah: Any particular proxy (nginx vs envoy) quirks?
[09:28] Jonah: Envoy has better gRPC streaming support; nginx needs chunked tuning. We'll share recommended config snippets.
[09:40] [10:00] Maya: Ok let's capture explicit acceptance criteria — Sarah?
[10:04] Sarah: 1) Ability to handle 100k-200k token contexts with 95th pct latency under 2.5s for small completions, 2) sustain bursts up to 1k rps with <1% permanent stream failures, 3) VPC peering + KMS + SOC2 fine.
[10:18] Maya: Noted. We'll map feature-to-SLA and include in the pilot.
[10:24] [10:40] Jonah: Quick note on tooling — Redwood Optimize suggests batching and serialization configs, and quantization levels per workload. For legal docs we often recommend float16 or int8 quant with an eval to ensure quality.
[10:56] Priya: Do you have eval tooling integrated? We need regression tests for model rollouts.
[11:00] Jonah: Yes, we have a per-prompt eval harness and can tie regressions to alerts; you can pin rollouts and canary test on a small % of traffic.
[11:14] Maya: We're coming up on time. Recap of next steps: send pricing + SOC2/VPC docs, Jonah to share benchmark scripts and short 3-day POC plan, Aperture to send traffic profiles and sample payloads.
[11:26] Sarah: Sounds good. One more ask — can you include a sample SLO / incident playbook? Last vendor didn't provide enough.
[11:32] Maya: We'll include that.
[11:35] Mark: Thanks everyone.
[11:36] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up by EOD tomorrow with docs and timeline.
[11:40] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional misheard words (e.g., "kv cache" appeared as "kayvee cache" in auto transcript), some timestamps approximate.
